interviewQuestions.question: Why can two different processes both think their code starts at 0x400000?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because logical addresses are per-process fictions, not physical facts. Every process gets its own logical address space, and the CPU's MMU translates every access that process makes through that process's own translation state — a base/limit pair in the simplest hardware, a page table in anything modern.

So when both processes issue an access to 0x400000, the MMU is consulting two completely different mappings. One might resolve to physical address 0x14000000, the other to 0x2A000000. The CPU never lets user code see or touch a physical address directly, so from inside either process there's no way to even notice the collision — because there isn't one at the hardware level.

I'd tie this back to why it matters: this is what makes multiprogramming safe. If addresses were physical, the compiler would have to know at build time exactly where in RAM the program would run, which is impossible once many programs share one machine. Address spaces are what let every compiler pretend it owns the whole machine.

**Testing:** whether you understand address spaces as a translation illusion maintained by hardware, not a coincidence or a shared-memory bug.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why two processes share an address

interviewQuestions.question: What are the three binding times, and why do almost all modern OSes use execution-time binding?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The three are compile time (the compiler bakes in absolute addresses, assuming a fixed load location), load time (the compiler emits relocatable offsets and the loader picks a base address once, at start), and execution time (translation happens on every single memory access, via the MMU, so the mapping can change while the program runs).

Modern OSes default to execution-time binding because everything we expect from a general-purpose system depends on being able to move a process's memory after it's already running: swapping a process out to disk and back, paging individual pages in and out on demand, and even just having the OS relocate memory to fight fragmentation. None of that is possible if the address was nailed down at compile or load time.

Concretely, when Linux swaps a page out under memory pressure and later brings it back at a different physical frame, it's relying entirely on execution-time binding — the process's logical addresses don't change, only what the page table says they map to. Compile-time binding basically only survives today in tiny embedded firmware or early-boot code that runs before any MMU is even configured.

**Testing:** whether you can connect an abstract classification to a concrete OS feature (swapping, paging) that depends on it.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Binding times and why execution-time wins

interviewQuestions.question: How does a base and limit register pair provide both relocation and memory protection with just two comparisons?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The base register holds where this process's memory region starts physically; the limit register holds how large that region is. Every logical address the process emits goes through the same two-step check: first, is the logical address less than the limit? If not, the hardware traps immediately — the process can never even construct a pointer that reaches outside its own region, which is the protection half.

If it passes, the physical address is just `base + logical` — one addition. That's the relocation half: the OS can load the same program at a different base address every time, or even move it later, and the program's own logical addresses never have to change, only the base register's value.

The elegance is that both properties fall out of the same tiny piece of state. The limitation is exactly what makes it too simple for real systems: it's one contiguous region per process, so there's no way to give code, stack, and heap different permissions, or to grow one without moving everything after it — which is why segmentation and paging replaced it in general-purpose OSes.

**Testing:** whether you can explain a simple mechanism precisely enough to also see its limits, not just recite that it exists.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Base/limit mechanics

interviewQuestions.question: How does execution-time address binding make ASLR possible, and why does that matter for security?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
ASLR needs the OS to place a process's stack, heap, and shared libraries at a different, randomized base address on every single launch, without touching the compiled binary. That's only possible because binding is deferred to execution time — the CPU translates every access through current MMU state, so the OS is free to choose that state fresh each run.

The security payoff is concrete: a memory-corruption bug like a buffer overflow is much less exploitable if the attacker can't predict where a useful piece of code (a "gadget" for return-oriented programming, or the address of `system()` in libc) actually landed. Without ASLR, an exploit can hardcode addresses and work reliably across machines; with it, a wrong guess just crashes the process instead of handing over control.

I'd also flag the limit: ASLR only works if binaries are compiled as position-independent (PIE) so the loader is actually free to relocate them, and it can be weakened by information leaks that reveal the randomized base at runtime — it raises the bar, it doesn't eliminate the bug class.

**Testing:** whether you can connect a low-level memory management mechanism to a security property, not just define ASLR in isolation.
